analysis|08-17|1916|Το κίνημα της Εθνικής Άμυνας|The National Defence movement|In the First World War King Constantine I wanted neutrality, while Venizelos supported entry on the side of the Entente. The disagreements led to the National Schism. In 1916 Bulgarian forces advanced into Eastern Macedonia, and the surrender of Fort Roupel provoked reactions. // On 17 August officers, on the initiative of Venizelos and with the support of the Allies, launched a movement in Thessaloniki and set up a revolutionary Committee of National Defence. Venizelos, Admiral Kountouriotis and General Danglis formed a Provisional Government. // The country was divided, with the state of Athens on the side of the king and Thessaloniki under Venizelos. The division lasted until 1917, when Constantine was forced to leave and Greece entered the war on the side of the Entente. The Schism left deep political wounds.

analysis|08-17|1944|Το Μπλόκο της Κοκκινιάς|The Kokkinia blockade|Kokkinia was a refugee district of Piraeus, with a strong resistance spirit and a large presence of EAM. In 1944, as the Occupation was nearing its end, the Germans and the Greek forces that collaborated with them, the Security Battalions, intensified measures against the resistance. // In the early hours of 17 August the Germans and the security battalion men surrounded the district and gathered the men at one point. Guided by local informers, they selected those regarded as suspect. Many were executed on the spot, and thousands were sent to camps, with further executions and deaths. // The blockade became one of the best-known crimes of the Occupation in Attica and a symbol of the Resistance. The district commemorates the memory with a monument and events every year. The event also recalls the role of the collaborators and the political division that followed in the Civil War.

analysis|08-18|1917|Η Μεγάλη Πυρκαγιά της Θεσσαλονίκης|The Great Fire of Thessaloniki|Thessaloniki was a large multicultural city, with a substantial Jewish community, and during the war years it hosted the Entente army. The houses were often wooden and crowded together, and in summer strong winds blew. The city had been incorporated into Greece in 1912. // The fire started in a house in the city and spread quickly, destroying the centre, the churches, the institutions and the neighbourhoods, and leaving about 70,000 people homeless. The Jewish community was particularly hard hit. // The destruction gave the opportunity for town-planning reconstruction. The Venizelos government entrusted the new plan to the French architect Ernest Hébrard and to an international committee, which gave the centre its broad form with squares and avenues. The fire permanently changed the image of Thessaloniki, and the composition of its population changed later too.

analysis|08-18|2004|Αγώνες σφαιροβολίας στην Αρχαία Ολυμπία|Shot put competition at ancient Olympia|The ancient Olympic Games were held at Olympia, in the sanctuary's stadium, until they were abolished in late antiquity. The modern Games began in 1896 in Athens, without events at Olympia. // For the 2004 Games it was decided that the shot put, for women and men, would be held in the ancient stadium of Olympia, as a symbolic link with antiquity. The stadium hosted the athletes before spectators seated on the slopes. // It was the first time since antiquity that an event of the official programme of the Games took place at the original site. The event attracted interest and highlighted the spirit of the Games' heritage. The stadium has since always had the possibility of hosting sporting activities, and the experience also prompted discussion on the conditions for holding events at archaeological sites.

analysis|08-19|1928|Εκλογές με νικητή τον Βενιζέλο|Elections won by Venizelos|In the late 1920s Greece had gone through a period of intense political instability, with coups, the dictatorship of Pangalos and continuous changes of government. Venizelos, who had withdrawn after 1920, returned to politics in 1928 and led the Liberal Party. // In the elections of August 1928 his party won an overwhelming majority, with a very high share and a large number of seats in Parliament. Venizelos formed a government and began a four-year period of reforms, which was the only completed parliamentary term of the era. // The government worked for reconstruction, with infrastructure works, educational reform, better relations with neighbours, such as the friendship agreement with Turkey in 1930 and with Italy. The world economic crisis, however, affected Greece, and in the elections of 1932 the party lost ground. The period is regarded as one of the most productive of interwar Greece.

analysis|08-19|1974|Δολοφονείται ο Αμερικανός πρέσβης Ρότζερ Ντέιβις|US ambassador Rodger Davies is murdered|After the Turkish invasion of Cyprus, public opinion in Cyprus and Greece was angry with the United States, which was held responsible for inaction or for the situation, especially given the role of Henry Kissinger. Many believed that Washington had tolerated the coup and the invasion. // On 19 August demonstrators gathered outside the American embassy in Nicosia. Shots hit the building, and the ambassador, Rodger Davies, who was in his office, was fatally wounded. A Cypriot employee of the embassy was also killed. Responsibility for the incident was attributed to members of EOKA B. // The murder created tension in relations between Cyprus and the United States and brought political violence to the fore. American diplomacy continued its efforts over the crisis, but the affair left a negative mark and kept alive discussion about the role of the United States in Cyprus.

analysis|08-20|1954|Η πρώτη προσφυγή της Ελλάδας στον ΟΗΕ για το Κυπριακό|Greece's first appeal to the UN on Cyprus|Cyprus was a British colony, and the demand for union with Greece was longstanding for the majority of Greek Cypriots. Britain refused to discuss the matter, regarding it as an internal question, and sought to maintain its strategic position in the Eastern Mediterranean, especially after its withdrawal from Egypt. // The Greek government of Alexandros Papagos, after consultations and under pressure from Makarios, submitted the request to the UN for the application of the principle of self-determination of peoples. The General Assembly decided not to discuss the matter. The same happened in the following years. // Despite the rejection, the Cyprus question became an international issue and was brought before the international community. The failure strengthened the conviction that another way was needed, and led to the start of the armed EOKA struggle in 1955. The matter also affected relations between Greece and Britain.

analysis|08-21|1866|Η Επαναστατική Συνέλευση της Κρήτης κηρύσσει την ένωση|The Cretan Revolutionary Assembly declares union|Crete was Ottoman and had already revolted in 1821, 1841 and 1858. In the 1860s the Christians demanded more rights and tax relief, and the Sublime Porte refused. The leadership of the Cretans was in the hands of strong personalities from Sfakia and the mountain areas. // In summer 1866 a General Assembly of the Cretans met, which asked for union with Greece, and an uprising followed that lasted until 1869. The date is by the old calendar. Greece supported the struggle with volunteers and ships that broke the blockade, such as the "Arkadi". // The Revolution of 1866 includes the holocaust of the Arkadi Monastery in November 1866, which shocked Europe. Despite the repression, the Great Powers were compelled to give Crete a new regime, the Organic Statute of 1868. Union was achieved in 1913.

analysis|08-21|1926|Το κίνημα Κονδύλη|The Kondylis movement|General Theodoros Pangalos had seized power by coup in 1925 and was a dictator in 1926, when he proclaimed himself President of the Republic. The situation was unpleasant for many, because of the authoritarian government and foreign policy, such as the clash with Bulgaria. // General Georgios Kondylis, a former prime minister, organised a military movement with the support of units. Pangalos was forced to resign and was arrested. Shortly afterwards an attempt was made to restore parliamentary normality. // Kondylis took over power temporarily, and then elections were called and a coalition government was formed. The period helped close the question of the Pangalos dictatorship, but political stability was not fully secured until 1928. The episode shows the power of the army in interwar politics.

analysis|08-22|1926|Ο Κονδύλης ανατρέπει τον Πάγκαλο|Kondylis overthrows Pangalos|After the Asia Minor Catastrophe and the fall of the monarchy, Greece experienced repeated coups and changes of regime. Theodoros Pangalos had governed as a dictator since June 1925, and in 1926 was proclaimed President of the Republic, but his popularity declined because of his policy and his clash with Bulgaria. // Georgios Kondylis, an officer who had taken part in developments of the period, organised a movement in August. Pangalos was deposed and imprisoned. Kondylis took over as prime minister in a transitional government and announced elections. // The overthrow opened the way for the elections of November 1926 and for a coalition government, and eventually for the political stabilisation that followed in 1928. The case shows the instability of the interwar period and the strong presence of the army in public life.

analysis|08-23|1864|Γεννιέται ο Ελευθέριος Βενιζέλος|Eleftherios Venizelos is born|Eleftherios Venizelos was born in Mournies of Chania, in Ottoman Crete, into a merchant family. The Revolution of 1866 marked his childhood, and his family took refuge for a time on Syros. The date of birth is by the old calendar. // He studied law in Athens and worked as a lawyer in Chania, and entered political life in the Cretan State. He led the Therisos movement in 1905 against Prince George and, in 1909, after the Goudi coup, was called to Athens and became prime minister in 1910. // As prime minister he led Greece through the Balkan Wars, which enlarged the country, and into the First World War. He clashed with King Constantine in the National Schism, and was the main representative of Greece in Paris in 1919. He lived until 1936, and his political legacy remains the subject of intense debate today.

analysis|08-24|1185|Οι Νορμανδοί καταλαμβάνουν τη Θεσσαλονίκη|The Normans take Thessaloniki|The Kingdom of Sicily, under Norman rule, had long had designs on the Balkans and the Byzantine Empire. After the death of Manuel I Komnenos in 1180, the empire passed into a period of instability, and Andronikos I came to the throne by violent means. The Normans saw an opportunity. // Their fleet and army landed at Durazzo and advanced on Thessaloniki, which they besieged and captured on 24 August after a short siege. Archbishop Eustathios, who described the events, records the violence and plundering of the inhabitants. // The Normans advanced towards Constantinople but were defeated by the army of the new emperor Isaac II Angelos at Demetritsi, and were forced to withdraw. The capture showed the weakness of the empire before 1204, and is an important source for Byzantine history thanks to the account of Eustathios.

analysis|08-25|1898|Η σφαγή του Ηρακλείου|The Heraklion massacre|Crete was in turmoil after the uprisings of 1896-1897 and the Greco-Turkish War of 1897. The Great Powers had sent troops to the island and administered areas. In Heraklion, where there was a large Muslim community, tension between the populations was high. // On 25 August by the old calendar a Muslim crowd attacked Christians and British soldiers during the collection of taxes, and massacres and destruction followed. Hundreds of Christians were killed, along with the British vice-consul and some soldiers. Britain responded with military force and the execution of those responsible. // The incident led the Powers to demand the withdrawal of Ottoman troops from Crete. In December 1898 Prince George arrived as High Commissioner of the Cretan State, and Crete gained autonomy, a forerunner of union with Greece in 1913.

analysis|08-25|1949|Η τελική επίθεση στον Γράμμο|The final attack on Grammos|The Civil War in Greece (1946-1949) had reached its final phase. The Democratic Army had fortified itself in the Grammos and Vitsi mountains, on the north-western borders. The National Army, with American aid and under the command of Alexandros Papagos, had been reinforced and improved its operations. At the same time the break between Tito and the Soviet Union had affected Yugoslavia's stance and the supply of the Democratic Army. // After the operation at Vitsi, the National Army attacked Grammos with infantry, artillery and air power, in the operation "Pyrsos". The battles lasted a few days, and the guerrillas were forced to withdraw towards Albania. // The defeat signalled the practical end of the Civil War. The KKE announced the cessation of hostilities on 16 October 1949. The war left thousands dead, refugees and deep political divisions in the country for decades.

analysis|08-26|1071|Η μάχη του Μαντζικέρτ|The battle of Manzikert|In the mid-11th century Byzantium had been weakened by internal disputes and by the neglect of the army of the frontier guards, while the Seljuk Turks made increasingly frequent raids in the East. This situation demanded immediate reaction from the empire. The battle of Manzikert was a great blow to the Byzantine Empire and its military system. // The emperor Romanos IV Diogenes organised a campaign to stop the pressure and met the army of the sultan Alp Arslan near Manzikert. The campaign was large, but its organisation had gaps. The capture of the emperor led to political disputes, which weakened the cohesion of power. // The Byzantine army was defeated and the emperor himself was taken prisoner. The defeat brought political instability to Constantinople, and in the following years the Turks gradually settled in the heart of Asia Minor. The battle is regarded as a milestone, because it started the long process by which the region passed from Byzantine to Turkish rule. The battle is cited as a turning point in the relationship of the Byzantines with the Seljuks and the East. The loss affected the military balance of the East for the following decades.

analysis|08-26|1922|Διαταγή για την εκκένωση της Μικράς Ασίας|Order to evacuate Asia Minor|In the preceding period the Greek army held a very long front line deep inside Asia Minor, far from its supply bases, and had been exhausted by years of war. The campaign had begun with the landing at Smyrna in 1919 and had reached the depths of the hinterland, without the resources to hold so open and vulnerable a line. // When the Turkish attack broke the front, the army found itself in retreat, and the leadership was forced to order the units to withdraw towards the coasts. The order had to be carried out in a landscape that the enemy controlled more and more, with roads full of people, animals and carts moving in the same direction. // The retreat took place in conditions of disorder, with soldiers and civilians moving towards Smyrna and the ports. The order in practice meant the end of the Greek presence in Asia Minor and foreshadowed the Asia Minor Catastrophe, with the uprooting of the Greek population that followed. The memory of this march remains a basic element of the refugee history of the country.

analysis|08-26|1922|Η τουρκική αντεπίθεση|The Turkish counter-offensive|After the Greek advance of 1921 the front had stabilised, with the Greek army tired, without reserves and without a clear political aim, while the Turks carefully organised their own attack under Mustafa Kemal. The attack began in the sector of Afyon Karahisar, where the Greek defence was vulnerable, and Kemal had concentrated significant superiority of forces at the point of rupture. // Within a few days the Greek positions were broken and the units began to retreat without being able to regroup. Command found it hard to co-ordinate the units retreating on different axes, and communications thinned out as the enemy advanced. // The counter-offensive decided the outcome of the war, since the retreat did not stop until the sea. It led to the fall of Smyrna and to one of the greatest refugee tragedies of modern Greek history. The Treaty of Lausanne of 1923 sealed the exchange of populations, with the Christians of Anatolia leaving for Greece and the Muslims of Greece migrating to Turkey.

analysis|08-27|1922|Ο Χρυσόστομος Σμύρνης θανατώνεται|Chrysostomos of Smyrna is killed|Chrysostomos was Metropolitan of Smyrna and a leading figure of the Greek Orthodox community of Asia Minor. When the Turkish army approached and the Greek officials were leaving, he chose to remain in the city close to his flock, despite pleas to leave. His stance was regarded by many as an act of pastoral responsibility, since he stayed beside people who could not leave. // After the entry of the Turkish forces he was arrested and handed over to a mob, which tortured and killed him in the streets of Smyrna. His death became a symbol of the sacrifice and martyrdom of Asia Minor Hellenism. Accounts of his last hours differ, so historians rely carefully on the sources. // The Orthodox Church later canonised him, and his memory is kept alive as an indication of the tragedy that followed the fall of the city. Smyrna then lost its multicultural identity, with the flight of the Greeks and Armenians who had lived there. His figure thus remains part of the collective history of the refugees.

analysis|08-29|1824|Ναυμαχία του Γέροντα|The naval battle of Gerontas|In 1824 the Ottoman fleet and the fleet of Muhammad Ali of Egypt were preparing operations against the islands that had revolted, after the destruction of Kasos and Psara. Those destructions had struck hard the naval centres of the islands and had shown the Porte that the Aegean could become a field of operations. The Greeks, with the ships of Hydra, Spetses and Psara, tried to intercept the enemy. // Off Gerontas, near Halicarnassus, the fleet under Andreas Miaoulis managed to inflict significant damage with fireships and forced the opponent to withdraw. Fireships, vessels filled with combustible materials that were steered onto the enemy, were a basic weapon of the Greek fleets during the Revolution. The tactic demanded courage and composure from the crews. // The victory showed that the Greek fleet remained a decisive factor of the war and delayed the Ottoman plans against the islands. The Peloponnese came under pressure later, however, when Ibrahim Pasha reached it in 1825, showing the limits of a naval victory on land. The naval battle remains one of the most characteristic acts of the naval Revolution.

analysis|08-29|1949|Τελειώνει ουσιαστικά ο Εμφύλιος|The Civil War effectively ends|In 1949 the government, with the support of the American aid programme and a reorganised army, went over to the attack, while the Democratic Army had been weakened by losses and internal disagreements. The Civil War had begun in 1946 between the government and the Democratic Army controlled by the KKE. The American aid, which had started with the Truman Doctrine in 1947, strengthened the government army and reorganised it. // The battles at Vitsi and Grammos ended with a victory for the government army, and the guerrillas crossed into Albania. Thus the major military operations ended, although small groups continued their activity for a while in the mountains. The war was one of the harshest conflicts of its era in Europe. // The war left behind thousands of dead, refugees and deep political division in Greek society. The defeat of the Democratic Army led to a long period of exclusion of the Left from public life. The wounds of the conflict appeared again in many later political crises.

analysis|08-29|2004|Λήξη των Ολυμπιακών Αγώνων της Αθήνας|The Athens Olympic Games close|Athens had taken on the 2004 Games and had prepared for years with major infrastructure projects, such as the metro, the new airport and the renovation of sports venues. The Games opened on 13 August and brought the Olympics back to the place where they had been reborn in 1896. The preparation changed the appearance of the city and its transport. // The closing ceremony was held at the Olympic Stadium. Greece completed the Games with 16 medals and 15th place, one of its best results. The Games were followed by a large worldwide audience, and the country was for a few weeks at the centre of international attention. // The event was regarded as organisationally successful and strengthened the country's image, while the cost and the later use of some facilities were discussed intensely. Many of the projects sought new uses after the Games, and the debate on the sustainability of the infrastructure remains open. 2004 thus remains a milestone for Athens.

analysis|08-30|1922|Η μάχη του Ντουμλουπινάρ|The battle of Dumlupinar|After the breakthrough of the Greek front at Afyon Karahisar, the Greek army retreated westwards and reached the heights around Dumlupinar. There an attempt was made to stabilise the defence and to protect the retreat towards the coasts. The position was critical, because the road to Smyrna passed through there and the command hoped to keep the enemy at bay. // The forces were tired, disorganised and to a large extent encircled, and the Turkish attacks broke up the Greek positions. The defeat signalled the end of any organised resistance in the interior. Those who were in the battlefield faced great difficulties in retreating, with shortages of food and ammunition. // From then on the Greek units moved towards Smyrna without hope of regrouping, and the Asia Minor campaign reached its tragic end. The collapse opened the way to the city and to the ports, where departure and the refugee crisis would follow. The battle is regarded as the point where the campaign definitively lost the initiative.

analysis|08-31|1971|Ο Γρίβας επιστρέφει κρυφά στην Κύπρο|Grivas returns secretly to Cyprus|Georgios Grivas had led EOKA in the struggle against the British in 1955–59 and remained faithful to the ideal of union with Greece, which was the central demand of the struggle at that time. After the independence of 1960 he had come into rupture with President Makarios, who regarded union as unattainable under the international conditions of the era. Grivas now lived in Greece, far from the island, and their disagreement over the goal and strategy of the struggle lasted for years. // In 1971 he secretly returned to the island and began to organise EOKA B, with the aim of pressing for union and opposing Makarios. The activity of the organisation divided Cyprus into a climate of internal conflict among Greek Cypriots, which weakened the Cypriot state and the cohesion of society. These methods, which included violence against political opponents, increased mistrust and division. // The event is regarded as one of the preconditions of the 1974 crisis, which led to the coup of 15 July against Makarios and to the Turkish invasion a few days later. The island thus remained divided, with consequences that last to this day. Discussion about the responsibility of all sides continues, and the history of Grivas remains connected with the most controversial moments of the Cyprus problem.

analysis|09-01|1911|Το «Αβέρωφ» μπαίνει στην υπηρεσία του Πολεμικού Ναυτικού|The "Averof" enters service with the navy|In the early 20th century Greece wanted to strengthen its navy, as tension with the Ottoman Empire grew and the naval questions of the Aegean had become urgent. The benefactor Georgios Averof, with his donation, contributed to the purchase of a modern armoured cruiser, which was built in Italy. The donation showed that national defence could also rest on the private benefaction of Greeks of the era. // The ship arrived in Greece and became the flagship of the fleet. In the Balkan Wars it was the most powerful ship of the Greek fleet and helped Greece to dominate the Aegean. Its presence strengthened the self-confidence of the crew and of the command, and its influence on the naval battlefields of the wars was significant. // Today the "Averof" survives as a museum ship at Faliro and is a symbol of the country's naval tradition. As a museum it is visited by pupils, historians and travellers, and its preservation shows how naval history is linked with national memory. The ship reminds us that naval strength was one of the basic tools of Greek policy at the beginning of the century.

analysis|09-01|1946|Το δημοψήφισμα για το πολίτευμα|The referendum on the form of government|After the Occupation Greece was deeply divided, and the question of the form of government remained open. King George II was abroad, and the elections of March 1946 had given victory to the right-wing parties, which called for a referendum. The question was linked with the wider confrontation between Right and Left that had broken out during the Occupation. // In the referendum the majority of voters favoured the return of the king. The result was disputed, because it took place in a climate of intense polarisation and violence, in the midst of the beginning of the Civil War. The Left, which had called for abstention, regarded the procedure as not free and as not reflecting the will of all citizens. // The king returned, but the question of the regime remained a source of division until the abolition of the monarchy in 1974. The referendum of December 1974 finally chose the form of a parliamentary republic. The period left deep marks on the relationship of society with the institutions.

analysis|09-01|1959|Αποφασίζεται η Α΄ Εθνική κατηγορία ποδοσφαίρου|The decision for the Greek first division football league|Until the late 1950s Greek football was organised mainly in local championships, while the national title was decided by a final stage between the winners of the regional associations. This made continuity and professional development of the sport difficult, since the clubs played few matches a year. The institutional character of the competitions was limited. // The general assembly of the Hellenic Football Federation decided to create a unified national division with regular matches between the clubs. The championship that started the following month gave a stable framework of organisation and increased public interest. The participation of clubs from different regions gave the sport a new national dimension. // The championship became the basis of modern Greek football, with the development of academies, professional clubs and television coverage. The First Division became one of the most stable competitions in the country and kept its popularity for decades. Its history begins with that decision of the Federation.

analysis|09-02|-31|Η ναυμαχία του Ακτίου|The battle of Actium|After the murder of Julius Caesar his successors fought for power. Octavian and Mark Antony had initially shared control of the Roman Republic together with Lepidus, but their rivalry, together with Antony's relationship with the queen of Egypt, Cleopatra, led to open war. The conflict had a political and ideological character, since each presented himself as the defender of Rome. // The naval battle took place off Actium, in the Ambracian Gulf. The fleet of Antony and Cleopatra was defeated, and both fled to Egypt, where they committed suicide shortly afterwards. The victory was decided to a large extent by Octavian's general Agrippa, who commanded the fleet of the victors. // Octavian remained sole master and became the first emperor of Rome, Augustus. The victory closed the age of the civil wars of the Republic and opened the period of the Roman Empire. Augustus gave power an institutional framework, which influenced the government of Rome for centuries.

analysis|09-02|1822|Οι Σουλιώτες φεύγουν από το Σούλι|The Souliotes leave Souli|The Souliotes had resisted for years against Ali Pasha of Ioannina, but in 1803 they had abandoned Souli and later returned with the Revolution. Epirus was the field of a long struggle between the local bodies and Ottoman authority. In 1822 Kesir Ahmet Pasha besieged the Souliotes, who had been reduced to a difficult position and lacked enough food and ammunition. // After negotiations they agreed to leave their villages with safe passage and went to the Ionian Islands, which were under British protection. The agreement secured their lives, but meant leaving the land where they had lived for centuries. The Ionian Islands were then a Greek-speaking centre with a strong tradition of philhellenism. // The uprooting was a significant loss for Epirus, but many of them continued to fight in the Revolution in other areas of Greece, such as Markos Botsaris. Souli thus became one of the symbols of heroic resistance, and the story of the Souliotes is honoured as an example of courage.

analysis|09-02|1944|Η σφαγή του Χορτιάτη|The Chortiatis massacre|During the Occupation the resistance also operated in the area of Thessaloniki, and the German forces responded with reprisals against civilians. In summer 1944, as the Wehrmacht was already on the defensive, attacks against the Germans on the outskirts of the city multiplied. This pressure led the occupation forces to an increasingly harsh treatment of the population. // On 2 September the Germans surrounded Chortiatis, killed 147 residents and burned the village. The dead were mainly civilians, among them women and children. The operation belongs to the pattern of reprisals that the Germans applied in many parts of Greece in order to discourage the resistance. // The massacre became one of the symbols of German barbarity in Macedonia, and the village is honoured as a martyr village. Its memory is kept every year with events that recall the victims. The history of Chortiatis thus belongs to the body of the country's martyr places, and the responsibility for the reprisals remains recorded.

analysis|09-02|1958|Η μάχη στον Αχυρώνα|The battle at Achyrona|In the EOKA struggle against the British, the fighters often hid in barns, houses and hideouts in the villages, with the help of residents who supported them. In 1958 the British authorities had intensified their operations to dismantle the organisation. The hidden life of the fighters was difficult and dangerous, and any hideout could become a trap. // At Liopetri in Famagusta a group of fighters hid in a barn and was surrounded by the British. In the clash that followed several members of EOKA were killed, and the place became a memorial of the struggle. The episode shows how hard the last years of the conflict were for the fighters. // The battle is regarded as one of the most bloody of the armed struggle and is honoured in Cyprus today as a sign of sacrifice for freedom. The story of the barn reminds us that the EOKA struggle cost lives, and that its memory is a basic element of the Cypriot national narrative.

analysis|09-03|1843|Η επανάσταση της 3ης Σεπτεμβρίου|The revolution of 3 September|From the arrival of Otto in 1833 Greece was governed as an absolute monarchy, although during the Revolution he had promised a constitutional regime. Discontent with the presence of Bavarians in power and with the economic situation grew, and politicians who had played leading roles in the Struggle pressed for change. The chief demand of the protesters was the limitation of the king's power. // In the night of 2 to 3 September Colonel Dimitrios Kallergis gathered the army in Athens, together with the people, and they demanded a constitution from Otto. The movement was one of the first examples of collective political pressure that combined army and citizens. The king yielded without bloodshed. // A National Assembly was elected, and the Constitution of 1844 established constitutional monarchy and Parliament. The revolution showed that the institutions of the state could be changed by political pressure. The constitutional monarchy that followed remained a basic element of Greek political life in the 19th century.

analysis|09-03|1974|Ιδρύεται το ΠΑΣΟΚ|PASOK is founded|After the fall of the dictatorship in the summer of 1974 Greece was returning to democracy, and new parties were taking shape. Andreas Papandreou, who had lived abroad during the years of the junta and had clashed with the regime, returned to Greece. His return took place in a climate of great expectation for change in political life. // He announced the founding of the Panhellenic Socialist Movement, with programmatic principles such as national independence, popular sovereignty and social liberation. The movement addressed broad popular circles, and its link with the anti-dictatorship resistance strengthened its credibility. // PASOK grew rapidly and in 1981 won the elections, bringing to power for the first time the Left of the social-democratic tradition. It became one of the two large parties of the Metapolitefsi, together with New Democracy. The pair of the two parties shaped Greek politics for decades.

analysis|09-04|1828|Οι Αιγυπτιακές δυνάμεις αρχίζουν να φεύγουν από την Πελοπόννησο|The Egyptian forces begin to leave the Peloponnese|From 1825 Ibrahim Pasha, son of Muhammad Ali of Egypt, held a large part of the Peloponnese and had caused great destruction. His campaigns had struck crops, villages and populations, with the aim of crushing the Revolution at its core. After the naval battle of Navarino in 1827 his position became difficult, since his fleet had been destroyed and his supplies were uncertain. // In 1828 the French general Maison arrived with a French expeditionary force, and under an agreement with the British admiral Codrington Ibrahim agreed to withdraw with his troops. The intervention was part of the wider international policy for Greece after Navarino, and the agreement avoided further conflict. The Ottoman fortresses remained under Ottoman control until they were handed over to the French. // The withdrawal of Ibrahim meant the end of foreign military presence in most of the Peloponnese. Kapodistrias, who had been governor since 1828, was thus able to begin the work of organising the state in a region that had suffered deeply. The Peloponnese became the core of the new Greek state.
